prime.problem: Having read 24 cards is not the same as being able to explain the system to a colleague in a minute. Recognising the right answer when you see it feels like knowing it; producing it cold, with a mechanism, a number and a trade-off, is the real test.
prime.fits: The course's last card and its self-test. It asks the three concept questions the course was built to answer (bottlenecks, the KV cache, throughput), each drawn from the group 1 cards and the levers card, and ends with ten rapid-fire questions across batching, data structures, scheduling and system design.
expect: one root sentence: one shared weight read + per-request KV
three 60-second answers with a mental model each
the common wrong answer for each
prime.goal: Answer each of the three big questions out loud in about a minute, naming the mechanism, one number and the trade-off, then handle the follow-ups without notes.

attend: Which single sentence generates all three answers, and which part of it does each answer lean on?
For each common wrong answer, which term of the step formula does it ignore?
Why does "a bigger batch is always better" fail even before memory runs out?
Which rapid-fire question tests data-structure cost rather than performance?
The card says knowing when a lever doesn't apply is part of explaining it. Which lever doesn't apply to a laptop with one user?

must: Every step reads all 16.06 GB of weights once, shared by every token → plus each request's own KV, which must fit in what's left → bottlenecks are about which read (or the math) is largest, the KV cache is the per-request part, and throughput levers either fill the shared read or shrink one of the reads

Bottlenecks: name the phase, then the term → decode at B = 1 is weight-bandwidth-bound (205 tok/s, 0.33% MFU) → at full batch the KV read (80%) and KV capacity (238 at 2k) bind → prefill is compute-bound

KV cache: fixed K and V per past token → O(n) decode instead of O(n²) → 128 KiB per token → capacity caps the batch and its read dominates a full step → so the scheduler's real job is managing KV blocks

Throughput: tokens per step ÷ step time → batching (49×), kept full by continuous batching (≈ 10×), then fewer bytes (FP8 KV 1.67×), less work (prefix caching), less overhead, more GPUs → maximise goodput under the SLO, not raw tok/s
elevated: A good explanation is mechanism, one number, the trade-off, then stop → lists of techniques and numbers without mechanisms don't transfer to another setup
reference: the exact wording of the 60-second answers
the category labels on the rapid-fire questions
the course's research sources, already cited on the earlier cards

compress.prompt: Without the card, say the root sentence out loud, then give each of the three 60-second answers in about a minute each. Record or write them, then check each against: mechanism named, one number, trade-off stated.
checklist: root: one shared weight read per step plus per-request KV that must fit
Q1: decode bandwidth-bound (4.9 ms, 205 tok/s), prefill compute-bound, KV capacity and KV read at full batch, CPU and stalls
Q2: K, V per token per layer per head; O(n) vs O(n²); 128 KiB; 238 sequences at 2k; 80% of a full step
Q3: batching 49× kept full by continuous batching; FP8 KV, prefix caching, chunking; goodput not tok/s
each answer names what it costs

retrieve.q: Explain, as if to a colleague, why buying a GPU with twice the FLOPs doesn't speed up single-user decoding, and what would.
answer: the step is max(0.016 ms math, 4.79 ms weight read) + 0.08 ms KV
twice the FLOPs leaves it at 4.9 ms
what helps: batching, quantization, speculative decoding, or more bandwidth

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens when the KV cache is full and a running request needs one more block.
answer: admission already stopped: waiting requests stay queued even with a free seat
the scheduler preempts (vLLM: the newest running request), frees its blocks, resets its computed count
it goes to the front of the queue and is recomputed later; too little memory means thrashing (e.g. 270 preemptions at 2,000 blocks)

retrieve.q: A colleague says "batch as big as memory allows, always". Give the counter-argument with numbers and say when they'd be right.
answer: each user slows (205 → 42 tok/s at 238) and TPOT grows toward the SLO
past capacity more tok/s means less goodput (60 req/s: 9,102 tok/s, 41% in SLO)
they're right for offline jobs with no latency target

compare.q: The overview answers the three questions in one line each; this card asks you to produce them. What does producing them expose that reading the overview doesn't?
answer: which numbers you can't recall and which mechanisms you can't chain
whether you can say the trade-off, not just the win
the overview is the map to check against after answering

compare.q: Course 5's last checkpoint also mixes per-request work questions. How does interleaving questions from different cards differ from answering this card's three questions in order, and why do both help?
answer: interleaving forces you to decide which concept applies before answering
the three questions in order rehearse complete, spoken explanations
together: pick the right model, then explain it fully

predict.q: Your colleague's setup is Llama-3.1-8B on the same H100 but every context is 8k. Before looking: how does your 60-second answer to question 1 change?
predict.answer: The shape stays, the numbers move toward KV. Only 59 sequences fit, not 238, and at that cap the step is still about 23.7 ms because the KV read (18.9 ms) is most of it, so full-batch decode gives about 2,489 tok/s instead of 9,973. Decode intensity can never pass 15.0 at 8k, so KV capacity and KV reads are even more clearly the bottleneck, and FP8 KV or GQA-style levers matter more.

apply.task: Record yourself giving the three 60-second answers without notes, then transcribe them. For each, mark whether you named the mechanism, gave at least one correct number, and stated a trade-off, and time it. Then answer the ten rapid-fire questions in writing before opening any, and list the cards to reopen for each one you missed.
apply.done: Each answer takes 45–90 seconds and ticks all three boxes (mechanism, a correct number such as 205 tok/s, 128 KiB or 49×, and a cost). You have a written list mapping every missed rapid-fire question to one card to reopen.
apply.hint: If an answer runs past 90 seconds, you are listing techniques; go back to the root sentence.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: how the 8k case changes question 1?
Which of the three answers couldn't you explain cleanly without notes?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: KV capacity → batch size → throughput, or KV read → step time → per-user speed?
Which rapid-fire question did you answer from the wrong card? That confusion is the comparison to redo.
Which card will you reopen first, and when will you retry the three questions?
